header: IN THE HIGH COURT OF SINDH, CIRCUIT COURT, MIRPURKHAS
Criminal Acquittal Appeal No. S-47 of 2025
Sht. Manoon v. Fida Hussain and others
body: ZULFIQAR ALI SANGI, J. Through this criminal acquittal appeal, the appellant/complainant has assailed the judgment dated 30.09.2025, passed by the learned Civil Judge and Judicial Magistrate, Nangarparkar, in Old Criminal Case No.136 of 2024, New Criminal Case No.61 of 2025, arising out of Crime No.22 of 2024, registered at Police Station Dano Dandhal, for offences punishable under Sections 147, 148, 149, 114, 506(ii), 504, 354, 337-A(i), 337-A(ii), 337-F(i) and 337-L(ii), PPC, whereby the respondents/accused were acquitted of the charge under Section 245(1), Cr.P.C.

2. The prosecution case, as set forth in the FIR lodged by the appellant/complainant Sht. Manoon, wife of Mano, is that on 17.07.2024, at about 03:00 p.m., she, her husband Mano and their son Khatu were working on their agricultural land bearing Survey No.78, when the respondents/accused, namely, Fida Hussain son of Khan Muhammad, Gulan son of Khan Muhammad, Nale Mitho son of Khan Muhammad, Arshad Ali Shah son of Mehboob, Ali Hassan son of Inayat, Gul Hassan son of Inayat, Sofan Shah son of Ali Ahmed, Taswar Ali son of Khan Muhammad, Taj Muhammad son of Ali Ahmed and Talib son of Ghulam Hussain, all residents of village Misri Shah, armed with hatchets and lathies, allegedly formed an unlawful assembly and entered upon their land. They allegedly abused the complainant party and questioned their right to cultivate the land, whereupon the complainant party asserted that the land belonged to their ancestors. At that juncture, accused Fida Hussain allegedly instigated his companions to assault the complainant party, pursuant to which all the accused allegedly attacked them. It was alleged that Hussan Shah inflicted a lathi blow upon the head of the complainant and dragged her by her hair, tearing her clothing; accused Gulan Shah inflicted a hatchet blow upon the head of Khatu, whereas accused Ali Hassan Shah caused a hatchet blow to the right arm of Mano. The remaining accused allegedly assaulted them with lathies, kicks and fists. Upon raising hue and cry, the accused allegedly departed from the place of occurrence while extending threats of murder in case the complainant party continued cultivating the land. The complainant party thereafter arranged transportation, obtained a police letter from Police Station Dano Dandhal, proceeded for medical treatment and, after the matter was allegedly not resolved through village notables, approached the Court through an application under Section 22-A, Cr.P.C., pursuant to which the FIR was registered.

3. After completion of investigation, the final report under Section 173, Cr.P.C. was submitted before the competent Court. Since Section 354, PPC, was then included in the schedule of the Anti-Rape (Investigation and Trial) Act, 2021, the record of the case was forwarded to the District and Sessions Court, Tharparkar at Mithi, vide order dated 04.10.2024. The competent Court took cognizance of the matter, supplied copies of the relevant documents to the accused and framed charge against them. Subsequently, vide order dated 23.07.2025, the learned Special Court/Additional Sessions Court-I, Tharparkar at Mithi, observed that, in view of the amendment in the Anti-Rape (Investigation and Trial) Act, 2021, whereby Section 354, PPC, had been excluded from the schedule, the case no longer fell within its jurisdiction and the record was returned to the competent Magistrate for proceedings in accordance with law. Thereafter, a fresh charge was framed against the respondents/accused under Section 242, Cr.P.C., to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

4. In order to substantiate its case, the prosecution examined the complainant Sht. Manoon as PW-01 at Ex.08, who produced the relevant letter and order dated 10.09.2024 passed by the learned District and Sessions Court, Tharparkar at Mithi, at Ex.8/A and Ex.8/B, along with the carbon copy of FIR at Ex.8/C. PW-02 Khatu, an injured witness, was examined at Ex.09, whereas PW-03 Mano, also an injured witness, was examined at Ex.10. PW-04 SIP Lal Malook was examined at Ex.11 and produced relevant police entries, memo of injuries and police letter at Ex.11/A to Ex.11/C. PW-05 Sanbhu, the mashir, was examined at Ex.12. PW-06 SIP Punhon Mal, the Investigating Officer, was examined at Ex.13 and produced relevant entries and the memo of site inspection at Ex.13/A to Ex.13/D. Subsequently, an application under Section 540, Cr.P.C. was moved by the learned ADPP for summoning Dr. Santosh as a prosecution witness, which was allowed vide order dated 30.08.2025 at Ex.15. Accordingly, PW-07 Dr. Indra, Woman Medical Officer, was examined at Ex.16 and produced the relevant police letter, provisional medico-legal certificate, referral letter, X-ray films, X-ray report, radiologist's opinion and final medico-legal certificate relating to complainant Sht. Manoon at Ex.16/A to Ex.16/J. PW-08 Dr. Santosh, Woman Medical Officer, was examined at Ex.17 and produced the relevant police letter, provisional medico-legal certificate, referral letter, X-ray films, X-ray report, radiologist's opinion and final medico-legal certificates pertaining to injured Khatu and Mano at Ex.17/A to Ex.17/M. Thereafter, the prosecution closed its evidence vide statement recorded at Ex.18.

5. The statements of the respondents/accused were recorded under Section 342, Cr.P.C., at Ex.19 to Ex.29, wherein they denied the allegations levelled against them, claimed false implication and pleaded innocence. They, however, neither opted to make statements on oath under Section 340(2), Cr.P.C., nor produced any defence witness or documentary evidence in support of their plea.

6. Learned counsel for the appellant/complainant contended that the impugned judgment is contrary to the evidence available on record and the law governing criminal trials. He submitted that the learned trial Court failed to appreciate the testimony of the complainant and the two injured witnesses in its true perspective, particularly when their presence at the place of occurrence was natural and their injuries stood corroborated by the medical evidence produced by the prosecution. He further argued that the discrepancies pointed out by the learned trial Court regarding the time of arrival at the police station and hospital were minor in nature, attributable to the circumstances prevailing after the occurrence and could not be treated as sufficient grounds to discard the otherwise consistent evidence of the injured witnesses. According to learned counsel, the medical evidence lends substantial corroboration to the ocular account, and the learned trial Court adopted an overly technical approach while extending the benefit of doubt to the respondents/accused. He prayed that the impugned judgment be set aside and the respondents/accused be dealt with in accordance with law.

7. Conversely, learned Deputy Prosecutor General supported the impugned judgment and contended that the learned trial Court had examined the prosecution evidence in its entirety and recorded acquittal after identifying material discrepancies and inconsistencies in the testimonies of the prosecution witnesses. He submitted that the acquittal recorded by the learned trial Court is based upon proper appreciation of evidence and does not suffer from any illegality, perversity or misreading of the record warranting interference by this Court in its appellate jurisdiction. He, therefore, prayed for dismissal of the appeal.

8. I have heard learned counsel for the appellant and learned Deputy Prosecutor General and have carefully examined the record as well as the impugned judgment. The principal question requiring consideration is whether the reasons assigned by the learned trial Court for acquitting the respondents/accused are legally sustainable and whether the impugned judgment suffers from any such misreading or non-reading of evidence, perversity or material illegality as would justify interference by this Court in an appeal against acquittal.

9. It is an established principle of criminal jurisprudence that an appeal against acquittal is to be considered with due caution and restraint. The acquittal recorded by a trial Court carries with it a reinforced presumption of innocence, and the appellate Court is not justified in reversing such acquittal merely because another view of the evidence may be possible. Interference is warranted only where the judgment of acquittal is found to be perverse, arbitrary, based upon misreading or non-reading of material evidence, or where the conclusions drawn by the trial Court are manifestly unreasonable and contrary to the settled principles of law. Where the view taken by the trial Court is a plausible view emerging from the evidence on record, the same ordinarily ought not to be disturbed.

10. In the instant case, the learned trial Court, while recording acquittal, has specifically examined the evidence of the complainant Sht. Manoon, injured witnesses Khatu and Mano, mashir Sanbhu, the police witnesses and the medical officers. The reasons assigned by the learned trial Court, particularly those reflected in paragraph No.21 of the impugned judgment, indicate that the acquittal was not recorded merely on the basis of insignificant or isolated discrepancies; rather, the Court considered the cumulative effect of the inconsistencies emerging from the prosecution evidence concerning the presence of witnesses at the place of occurrence, the manner in which the injured persons were allegedly taken away from the scene, their subsequent movement towards the police station and hospital, and the varying accounts regarding the time of their arrival at different places.

11. The record reflects that the complainant, PW-02 Khatu and PW-03 Mano furnished differing accounts regarding the time when they allegedly reached Police Station Dano Dandhal and the hospital for medical treatment. The complainant stated that they reached the police station after sunset, whereas PW-02 Khatu stated that they had reached the police station before sunset. PW-03 Mano, on the other hand, stated that they reached the police station at about 08:00 to 08:30 p.m. Such accounts were not found consistent with the relevant police entry and memo of injuries, which reflect the arrival of the complainant party at 21:50 hours. Similarly, the prosecution witnesses furnished varying accounts regarding the time of their arrival at the hospital, which also did not correspond with the times recorded by the medical officers in the relevant medico-legal documents. These discrepancies, when examined in isolation, may not necessarily be sufficient to discard the testimony of an injured witness. However, the question is whether, in the peculiar circumstances of the case, the inconsistencies collectively affect the reliability of the prosecution narrative. The learned trial Court was required to examine the entire evidence and assess whether the prosecution had succeeded in establishing the charge beyond reasonable doubt. Upon such examination, the learned trial Court found the discrepancies to be material in the context of the overall prosecution case. The said conclusion, having emerged from an assessment of the evidence available on record, cannot be termed arbitrary or unreasonable.

12. It is equally true that the testimony of an injured witness ordinarily carries considerable evidentiary weight, as the presence of such witness at the scene of occurrence is generally established by the fact of sustaining injuries during the incident. However, the status of an injured witness does not render his or her testimony immune from scrutiny. The evidence of an injured witness is required to be examined with the same judicial caution as any other evidence, particularly where material inconsistencies emerge regarding the occurrence, the conduct of the witnesses or the subsequent events. The medical evidence, although relevant and corroborative in nature, primarily establishes the nature and extent of injuries sustained by the injured persons; it does not, by itself, establish the identity of the assailants or the manner in which the injuries were caused. In the present case, the medical evidence confirms the existence of injuries, but the learned trial Court, upon evaluating the ocular account alongside the remaining evidence, found the prosecution case not sufficiently reliable to sustain a conviction.

13. Furthermore, the learned trial Court has also taken note of the discrepancy concerning the presence and role of mashir Sanbhu at the place of occurrence and during the subsequent events. His account regarding the presence of other women and children at the scene was not corroborated by the complainant and the other injured witnesses in the manner expected by the learned trial Court. The Court also considered the discrepancy regarding the manner in which the injured persons were allegedly removed from the place of occurrence, as well as the role attributed to Sanbhu in accompanying or assisting them thereafter. These circumstances, when considered alongside the discrepancies regarding the timings of the occurrence and subsequent events, were found by the learned trial Court to create uncertainty in the prosecution version. It is not the function of this Court in an appeal against acquittal to substitute its own assessment merely because a different interpretation of such evidence is conceivable, unless the findings of the trial Court are shown to be wholly unreasonable or legally unsustainable.

14. The settled principle of law is that the prosecution is required to establish the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt, and the accused is entitled to the benefit of every reasonable doubt arising from the evidence. Such benefit is not a concession or favour extended to the accused but a right flowing from the fundamental principle of criminal justice. Even a single reasonable doubt, if arising from the evidence and affecting the prosecution case, is sufficient to entitle an accused to acquittal. The learned trial Court, after considering the material contradictions and inconsistencies in the prosecution evidence, concluded that the prosecution had failed to establish the guilt of the respondents/accused beyond reasonable doubt. The said conclusion is supported by the material available on record and cannot be said to be the result of arbitrary exercise of judicial discretion.

15. In view of the foregoing discussion, I find that the impugned judgment does not suffer from any illegality, perversity, misreading or non-reading of evidence warranting interference by this Court. The appellant has failed to demonstrate any compelling circumstance justifying reversal of the acquittal recorded by the learned trial Court. The findings recorded by the learned trial Court are based upon an assessment of the evidence and constitute a plausible view of the case. Consequently, the impugned judgment merits no interference.

16. Accordingly, this criminal acquittal appeal is dismissed. The judgment dated 30.09.2025, passed by the learned Civil Judge and Judicial Magistrate, Nangarparkar, in Old Criminal Case No.136 of 2024, New Criminal Case No.61 of 2025, arising out of Crime No.22 of 2024, registered at Police Station Dano Dandhal, whereby the respondents/accused were acquitted under Section 245(1), Cr.P.C., is maintained.
17. The appeal stands disposed of accordingly.
